verdict: Caution — lend only to rooftop and small C&I EPC contractors with clean land title and proven collections; avoid utility-scale park EPC and land-dependent developers in Jaisalmer until the Oran land disputes clear.
title: Jaisalmer solar EPC & rooftop: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A solar EPC contractor buys modules, inverters, structure and cable, moves them to site, and converts them into an installed, commissioned plant for a customer who pays on milestone. **Modules alone are around 70% of total project cost [9], so the EPC firm is really a thin-margin assembler of someone else's expensive input.** Cash does not sit in the plant; it sits in retention money held back by the customer and in unbilled work-in-progress. **Retention held with customers forces dependence on bank working capital, and utilisation ran between 78% for the twelve months to November 2023 in one rated peer [9].** So when a proposal lands, check the retention percentage and the release schedule before anything else; if retention exceeds the margin, ask what funds the gap.

## Where value and cash actually sit
Pricing power is weak because competition is intense and regulatory shifts are frequent [10], and profitability is exposed to module price swings [9]. **The peer set shows the split clearly: Waaree Renewable grew revenue 36.53% to Rs 1,057.84 crore in Q2 FY27 while PAT fell nearly 30% to Rs 81.48 crore [6].** GK Energy grew H1 FY27 revenue 38.9% to Rs 907.8 crore with EBITDA up 21.6% to Rs 160.5 crore [5], but carries 204-day receivables [7]. **Growth without collection is the pattern to underwrite against, not to reward.** Capex is light for the EPC firm itself; the heavy capital sits with the developer, where debt-equity of 70:30 or 75:25 is typical [11].

## What has changed in Jaisalmer now
The constraint here is land, not demand. **The Rajasthan High Court has stayed felling of trees in the Oran area for a proposed solar project at Baiya village, Jaisalmer [1], and villagers have begun a 700 km foot march from the India-Pakistan border to Jaipur to protect sacred groves and pastures [2].** Activists claim 580,000 hectares of orans are wrongly classified as wastelands in revenue records [2], and a 400 MW solar park is proposed in a catchment local residents depend on [2]. **This is local news, not peer performance, and it is recent (March-April 2026).** The practical effect: utility-scale park EPC in this district can stall on clearances mid-execution. On the rooftop side, Rajasthan subsidy and JVVNL net-metering rules are the demand driver [3], but that source is a commercial directory, not an official policy document — collect the current subsidy order from customer.

## Who to pursue and how to grow safely
**Pursue rooftop and small commercial-and-industrial EPC contractors with a completed-project list, DISCOM approval letters in hand, and customers who pay on commissioning.** Pursue EPC firms serving pump and rooftop programmes where the order book is documented — GK Energy won a 1 lakh rooftop systems order and a 150 MW/300 MWh BESS order [5], which shows where volume is moving. **Avoid utility-scale park EPC and any borrower whose site depends on Oran or pasture land with pending revenue reclassification [2].** Structure against retention: take monthly stock and receivable statements, a project-wise retention register, and module purchase invoices.

## Early-warning signs
- **Receivables stretching past the peer benchmark of 204 days [7] -> stop fresh disbursement and review the account.**
- **Retention release slipping beyond the contract date [9] -> ask for the customer's payment confirmation in writing.**
- **Module price movement compressing margin below sanction assumption [9] -> re-price or reduce exposure.**
- **Any court stay or land objection on a project site [1][2] -> freeze that project's limit immediately.**
- **Working capital utilisation approaching the rated peer's 78% [9] -> require a fresh cash-flow statement before renewal.**
